extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis and humor theory; writers or analysts studying joke mechanisms
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Freud's model to analyze or construct jokes by identifying which of the three economy principles is at work, which joke-work techniques are used (condensation, displacement, conceptual), and whether a joke is innocent or tendentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Der Witz (the joke / wit) — economy of inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Der Witz (the joke / wit) — economy in the expenditure of inhibition. The joke smuggles forbidden content past the inner censor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke's pleasure comes from releasing inhibited material (forbidden thoughts, aggressive or sexual impulses) by evading the internal censor. If so, the laughter is partly the discharge of inhibition energy in addition to any technical wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Das Komische (the comic) — economy of thought/ideation
rubrics_metrics.description: Das Komische (the comic) — economy in the expenditure of thought / ideation. We laugh at mismatched movements, behavior, or appearance because we expended more mental energy than the object turned out to require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the humor arises from a perceived mismatch, error, or surplus of cognitive effort (e.g., a clumsy movement, incongruous behavior) rather than from forbidden content; the pleasure is primarily intellectual and generally smaller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Der Humor (humor proper) — economy of affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Der Humor (humor proper) — economy in the expenditure of affect. A situation that should distress us is reframed by the superego in a benevolent voice that says 'look at the dangers of this world; mere child's play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the humor functions to reframe threatening or distressing material so that affective expenditure is reduced — a liberating, consoling attitude (e.g., gallows humor). This involves a benevolent superego giving the ego permission to treat fear or sorrow lightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation: composite-word formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation with formation of composite word (e.g., 'famillionaire' — 'he treated me familionairely').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for portmanteaux or blended words that compress multiple meanings into one term; the condensed form yields the joke's dual readings and economy of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation: modification of a word to press two meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation with modification (slight alteration of a word so two meanings press together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify small phonetic or orthographic changes that allow a single utterance to evoke two related meanings simultaneously; the pleasure comes from the overlap of senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation: multiple use of same material
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple use of the same material — same word in different senses, in opposite senses, with full vs. modified meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when a word or phrase is reused within a joke in varied senses (literal vs. figurative, full vs. truncated meanings) to produce layered interpretations and comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement: displacement of accent (answering a different question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement of accent — answering a different question than the one apparently asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the punchline redirects emphasis to an unexpected element or responds to an implicit rather than explicit prompt; the shift displaces the intended sense and produces surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement: faulty reasoning enjoyed as faulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Faulty reasoning that is recognized as faulty but enjoyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot deliberate logical errors, non sequiturs, or sophistic moves that the listener recognizes as incorrect yet finds pleasurable — the enjoyment comes from the play with reasoning rather than its correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement: absurdity taken as sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity as sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note uses of apparent absurdity that are treated as meaningful within the joke's frame, producing laughter from the incongruity between sense and nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement: indirect representation (allusion, omission, allegory, imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect representation — using allusion, omission, allegory, or imagery to point at the forbidden idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the joke relies on insinuation or indirect cues to evoke taboo content; omission and allusion allow the forbidden idea to be suggested without explicit statement, enabling the censor to be bypassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement: representation by the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation by the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for jokes that invert or reverse roles, meanings, or expectations so that the objectionable content is conveyed via its opposite, facilitating a disguised release of inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual technique: unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Unification — connecting two distant ideas via a third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where an unexpected third element links two otherwise unrelated concepts, creating a surprising conceptual bridge that produces humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual technique: allusion via small detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusion via small detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for minor, seemingly incidental details that subtly point to a larger, often taboo meaning; the smallness of the cue increases the satisfaction when the connection is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual technique: comparison with surprising tertium
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison with surprising tertium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comparisons that introduce an unexpected 'third' element (tertium) to juxtapose two items, yielding a novel relation and comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual technique: outdoing wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Outdoing wit (the answer that goes one further than the provocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect punchlines that escalate beyond the provocation in an audacious or excessive way; the humor comes from the one-upmanship and the shock of surpassing expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent jokes — intellectual economy only
rubrics_metrics.description: Innocent jokes save intellectual expenditure only — pleasure is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify jokes whose amusement stems solely from cleverness, wordplay, or intellectual economy without smuggling forbidden content. Expect milder laughter and less release of inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendentious jokes — hostile and obscene purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendentious jokes carry one of two further purposes: hostile jokes (aggression against the target — replace impossible physical attack) and obscene jokes (sexual exposure of a target who would otherwise be unavailable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a joke serves an aggressive or sexualizing function toward a target; such jokes release inhibition energy in addition to technical pleasure and therefore produce larger laughs. Consider sub-classifying as 'hostile' (displacement of aggression) or 'obscene' (sexual exposure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-person structure of tendentious jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: First person: the joke-teller (who has the impulse). Second person: the target (who is being aggressed against or sexualized). Third person: the listener (whose laughter both grants permission and consummates the discharge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a tendentious joke, map these roles. Note that the teller cannot laugh at his own tendentious joke—the listener's laughter functions as the social discharge and permission for the teller's suppressed impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor proper as liberating/sublime (1928 essay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor in the strict sense has a liberating and sublime quality: the superego, normally severe, here treats the ego as a parent treats a child. The ego is reassured: 'Look at this thing that seemed so menacing; how trivial it is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to distinguish 'humor proper' that consoles or elevates rather than merely discharges inhibition. Examples include gallows humor where the threatened person reframes peril as trivial; the superego's benevolence is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for evaluating a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the laughter coming from technique alone (condensation/displacement)? Is there a forbidden content (hostile or sexual) being smuggled past the censor? If so, who is the implied target, and is the listener's laughter a permission grant? Or is this humor proper — a benevolent superego reframing a distressing situation as play?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these questions systematically to determine which economy (inhibition, thought, affect) and which techniques are operative, whether the joke is tendentious or innocent, who benefits from the discharge, and whether the social function is permission-granting or consolatory.
